class.name: NetwClockConfig
class.brief_description: Draft the session clock is initialized from, declared on a scope node.
class.description: [method Netw.configure_clock] returns a draft the scope node owns. Edit it in place or through the fluent methods, and the session copies its values once, at a deferred boundary after the declaring call stack has finished. From then on the clock holds owned values and this Resource is a spent authoring snapshot: a later setter reports the late write and moves nothing. [codeblock] func _init() -> void: Netw.configure_clock(self).tickrate(60).display_offset(2) [/codeblock] Consuming one also arms the session's AUTOMATIC pump: the clock advances on the [SceneTree]'s own physics frame, reading that frame's actual delta, and the session's poll advances nothing. The pump runs only while the session is mounted on a branch, its peer is connected, [constant NetwMultiplayer.CLOCK_PARAM_MANUAL_TICK] is off, the editor is not authoring and the tree is not paused, so a paused game's clock stands still and resumes without catching up. A manual driver still advances it deliberately with [method NetwMultiplayer.clock_physics_step]. [method NetwMultiplayer.clock_get_config] returns a detached snapshot of the running values. Live tuning goes through [method NetwMultiplayer.clock_set_param], which updates the engine and shows up in that snapshot without ever reopening this draft. Tickrate is not tunable that way: it is initialization. A preset handed to the verb is copied rather than kept, so one [code].tres[/code] may seed several scenes. [signal NetwMultiplayer.clock_configured] fires once, after consumption and runtime setup.
